name: Lithium iron phosphate
plain: A rechargeable lithium-ion type at 3.2 volts that lasts thousands of charges and resists overheating better than other common lithium-ion types. It stores less energy for its weight.
self_discharge: Elevated compared with other lithium-ion types (Battery University); no figure given
summary: Lithium iron phosphate (LFP or LiFePO4) batteries are lithium-ion batteries with an iron phosphate cathode and a graphite anode, giving 3.2 V nominal on an unusually flat curve. They trade energy density for thermal stability and long cycle life, and use neither nickel nor cobalt.
body:
## How it works

An LFP battery is a lithium-ion battery in which the positive electrode is lithium iron phosphate (LiFePO4) and the negative electrode is graphitic carbon on a metal backing. Lithium ions move between the two intercalation electrodes in the same way as in other lithium-ion batteries. The cathode material has a specific capacity of 170 mAh/g. Iron and phosphate are common in the Earth's crust, and the battery contains neither nickel nor cobalt.

## Discharge behavior

Nominal voltage is 3.2 V (Battery University gives 3.20 to 3.30 V), with a full charge at 3.60 to 3.65 V. Wikipedia lists a minimum discharge voltage of 2.0 to 2.8 V, and Battery University gives 2.50 V for full discharge and 2.00 V as the minimum. Wikipedia warns that a pack's protection system must keep every battery in it above 2.5 V to avoid severe damage in most cases. The open-circuit voltage is exceptionally flat between roughly 20% and 80% state of charge, so battery voltage says little about remaining charge across most of the working range.

Specific energy is lower than other common lithium-ion types: Battery University gives 90 to 120 Wh/kg, and Wikipedia gives 95 to 172 Wh/kg, noting a 2024 claim of 205 Wh/kg for a single battery, not a pack, from CATL. Cycle life is long. Battery University lists 1,000 to 2,000 cycles under ideal conditions and Wikipedia 2,500 to more than 9,000 depending on conditions. Battery University places thermal runaway at about 270 °C and describes the chemistry as safe at full charge; Wikipedia attributes this to thermal and chemical stability, since layered oxide cathodes such as lithium cobalt oxide and NMC release oxygen on heating while LFP generally decomposes at higher temperatures. LFP batteries can still catch fire under extreme conditions such as overcharging, very high temperatures or severe physical damage.

## Uses

Electric vehicles, utility-scale stationary storage and backup power, according to Wikipedia; Battery University lists stationary uses that need high current and endurance. Four LFP batteries in series give a nominal 12.8 V, close to a lead-acid battery with six batteries inside, so LFP is used as a lead-acid replacement in automotive and solar applications, provided the charging system does not apply excessive voltage. Battery University lists the 26650 cylindrical battery and prismatic batteries as typical packaging.

## History

John Goodenough first identified the polyanion class of lithium-ion cathode materials, and in 1996 Padhi et al. identified LiFePO4 as a member of that class for use in batteries. In 2022, Chinese manufacturers held a near-monopoly of LFP production, and key patents began to expire that year.

## Status

Current. IEC 61960-3 lists 3.2 V as the nominal voltage for iron phosphate systems and uses the positive-electrode code Fp (F alone means iron), so a strict IEC designation for a cylindrical battery with a carbon negative begins IFpR.
strengths: Thermal runaway near 270 °C, higher than other common lithium-ion types (Battery University)
Long cycle life: 2,500 to over 9,000 cycles depending on conditions (Wikipedia)
Flat voltage across most of its charge range
limitations: Lower specific energy than NMC and NCA
Flat voltage makes state of charge hard to read from voltage
Damaged by discharge below about 2.5 V in most cases
Elevated self-discharge for a lithium-ion type (Battery University)
safety: Can still catch fire from overcharging, very high temperature or severe physical damage
Packs need balancing across the batteries inside and a protection system that stops each one above 2.5 V
